# Test claims instead of trusting authority (`empiricism_over_authority`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by printing_press
- Core idea: The age or fame of an author is no evidence for a claim about nature; what counts is whether anyone can check it. Old books contain checkable errors: Aristotle writes that women have fewer teeth than men (count them), and that a body ten times heavier falls ten times faster (drop a large and a small stone together); Galen relied heavily on animal dissection and inferred unseen passages through the wall between the heart's chambers. The persuasive form inside an older worldview is not 'Aristotle was a fool' but 'Aristotle and Galen themselves observed and told us to trust the senses over arguments; we are doing what they did, with more cases'. Authority remains a sensible shortcut where you cannot check, which is why testimony must be ranked, not ignored.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming medieval scholars followed Aristotle blindly: scholastics disputed him constantly (Buridan, Oresme, the Paris condemnations of 1277)
  - Dismissing the authorities as stupid: Aristotle and Galen were excellent observers, and their opponents often had good arguments (no stellar parallax was measurable until 1838)
  - Attacking a university's or guild's textbook author in public attacks the livelihood of every local physician or master
  - Extending the argument to Scripture or to the classics of state ideology turns a dispute about nature into heresy or disloyalty
  - Asking people to distrust authority while demanding they trust the player without evidence
- History: india: by c. 8th c. AD – Carvaka materialists challenge scriptural authority and privilege perception; fragments quoted by critics show that some accepted inference grounded in ordinary experience; china: Warring States period – the Mozi lists what people have seen or heard among the tests of a doctrine; c. 80 AD Wang Chong, Lunheng, checks received stories against experience; greece: c. 350 BC – Aristotle: credit observation more than theories (Generation of Animals III.10); 2nd c. AD Galen urges readers to dissect for themselves; islamic: c. 900 – al-Razi, Doubts about Galen; early 11th c. Ibn al-Haytham, Doubts about Ptolemy (criticism of inherited astronomical models); c. 1200 Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi corrects Galen on the jawbone from skeletons in Egypt; europe: 1543 – Vesalius corrects Galen's anatomy from human dissection; 1660s Royal Society motto 'Nullius in verba' (take nobody's word for it)
- Read:
  - Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica (1543)
  - Ramkrishna Bhattacharya, From Proto-materialism to Materialism: The Indian Scenario (2016)
  - David Wootton, The Invention of Science: A New History of the Scientific Revolution (2015)
